Modern.brandNameRationale: Saddle-stitch (the staple binding through the spine fold) is the production signature of the zine — two staples, one fold, finished. Naming the press for the binding method places the brand on the most honest production fact of the form.
Modern.industrySummary: Indie publishing in the zine-adjacent space competes on visual swagger and editorial taste. There is room for a modern press that names itself after the binding method and runs everything in one format: 24 pages, two staples, one fold.
Modern.competitorLandscape: Microcosm Publishing (microcosmpublishing.com) holds the modern indie-press slot. Perfectly Acceptable Press (perfectlyacceptable.co) is the considered-design peer. Issue Press (issuepress.bigcartel.com) is the small-format precedent. We sit closer to Perfectly Acceptable, sharper on the format constraint.
Modern.positioningStatement: A modern indie press where every title is 24 pages, two staples, one fold.

targetAudience.primary: 25 to 40. Owns a stack of zines on the desk. Reads at the kitchen table. Will pay 8 dollars for a 24-page run of 200.
behaviors: Reads at the table, not the screen
Subscribes to one small press per year
Buys at zine fairs in person

dos: Print the page count on the cover
Publish a monthly issue, on time

Modern.logoDirection: A wordmark — Staple Bound set in a tight modern grotesk, with two small black bars to the left of the word standing in for the staples. The two bars alone are the favicon.

typography.primary: GT America for the wordmark and headlines
typography.secondary: GT America Mono for issue numbering and credits
typography.rationale: One family. The mono carries the issue data, the regular carries the press.

Luxury.brandNameRationale: Factsheet Five (1982–98) was the canonical directory of the zine world — Mike Gunderloy's review-of-everything, the central register that made the network legible. Factsheet Press places the imprint as the heritage cataloguer of the form, in archival editions.
Luxury.industrySummary: Luxury indie publishing is a small but durable segment served by a few archive-leaning houses. There is room for an imprint that takes the cataloguer's posture — boxed sets, archival reissues of significant zines, deeply researched introductions.
Luxury.competitorLandscape: Primary Information (primaryinformation.org) holds the archival small-press art slot. Siglio Press (sigliopress.com) is the considered-archive peer. Boo-Hooray (boo-hooray.com) is the zine-archive precedent. We sit between Siglio and Boo-Hooray, sharper on the directory tradition.
Luxury.positioningStatement: An archival imprint reissuing significant zines in boxed editions, with introductions.

targetAudience.primary: 40 to 70. Builds an archive of small-press print. Holds boxed editions on a separate shelf. Reads the introduction first.
behaviors: Reads the introduction before the zine

dos: Print the print run on the colophon
Cite the original printer and year

Luxury.logoDirection: A serif wordmark — Factsheet Press set in a high-contrast classical serif, with a small index-card rectangle as the hallmark, blind-embossed on every slipcase.

typography.primary: Canela for the wordmark and slipcase
typography.secondary: GT America Mono for colophons and edition numbering
typography.rationale: Canela carries the archival posture. The mono carries the production data.

Minimal.brandNameRationale: Mimeo is the shortened form of mimeograph — the duplicating machine that produced the great mid-century zine and small-press output. A five-letter coined word, the smallest possible signature for the smallest possible press.
Minimal.industrySummary: Minimal indie publishing competes on the radical economy of the object. A one-word press whose entire identity is the truncated name of the duplication method has no peer in restraint.
Minimal.competitorLandscape: Inventory Press (inventorypress.com) holds the considered-minimal small-press slot. Roma Publications (romapublications.org) is the minimal-art-publishing peer. Onomatopee (onomatopee.net) is the European precedent. We sit below all three on visual noise.
Minimal.positioningStatement: A minimal indie press named for the mimeograph.

targetAudience.primary: 28 to 45. Reads one zine a month. Buys from a small list of presses. Knows the difference between offset and risograph.
behaviors: Buys from a fixed list of presses
Reads slowly, one sitting per issue

dos: Print the issue number on the spine fold
Say nothing the colophon doesn't say

Minimal.logoDirection: A wordmark only — Mimeo in a single-weight grotesk, lowercase. The whole brand is the word. The favicon is a single black square the height of the type.

typography.secondary: Söhne Mono for credits and colophons
typography.rationale: One typeface family. The mono carries the publishing credits, the regular carries the press.

Corporate.brandNameRationale: Cut-and-paste is the literal layout method that produced the zine — scissors, glue stick, photocopier. Naming the press for the workflow puts the production method itself at the front of the brand.
Corporate.industrySummary: There is a corporate-feeling lane between a small press, a print broker, and a zine-fair organizer that no one is filling cleanly. A house that runs printing services for independent zinemakers and operates a small in-house imprint would sit alone.
Corporate.competitorLandscape: Newspaper Club (newspaperclub.com) holds the print-on-demand-for-small-runs slot. Mixam (mixam.com) is the zine-printing services peer. Lulu (lulu.com) sits in the institutional self-publishing middle. We sit between Newspaper Club and Mixam, with an imprint alongside.
Corporate.positioningStatement: Printing services and a small imprint for independent zinemakers.

targetAudience.primary: Independent zinemakers, small-press editors, and zine-fair organizers running print orders of 100 to 1,000.
behaviors: Orders short runs four times a year
Manages a fixed list of zine titles

dos: Speak to the maker, not the reader

Corporate.logoDirection: A wordmark with a hallmark — Cut and Paste Press set in a clean grotesk, paired with a small scissors-and-glue-stick pictogram reduced to two crossed strokes.

typography.primary: Aktiv Grotesk for the wordmark and headers
typography.secondary: Aktiv Grotesk for body and price lists
typography.rationale: One typeface family. Reads professional on a quote and clean on a print order.

Creative.brandNameRationale: Stapler Gang names the zine-fair assembly line — the kitchen-table crew that folds, staples, and trims a print run of 200 the night before the fair. The name puts the social fact of the form (zines are made by a group at a table) at the front.
Creative.industrySummary: The creative-zine segment is built around the zine fair, the open call, and the community table. There is room for an imprint built explicitly as a collective, with rotating editors and a quarterly open call for contributors.
Creative.competitorLandscape: Quimby's Bookstore (quimbys.com) holds the Chicago zine-community slot. Printed Matter (printedmatter.org) is the institutional small-press peer. People of Print (peopleofprint.com) is the network precedent. We sit between Quimby's and People of Print, sharper on the collective structure.
Creative.positioningStatement: A creative imprint run as a collective, with quarterly open calls and rotating editors.

targetAudience.primary: 22 to 40. Makes zines themselves. Tables at three fairs a year. Reads everyone else's zines first.
behaviors: Tables at zine fairs three times a year

dos: Print the contributor list on the back
Sign every copy by the editor of the issue

Creative.logoDirection: A hand-drawn wordmark — Stapler Gang lettered in a punk-zine brush face, framed by a thin saddle-stitched-booklet outline. The booklet outline alone is the favicon.

typography.primary: A punk-zine brush face for the wordmark
typography.secondary: GT America Mono for issue numbering and dates
typography.rationale: The brush face carries the collective voice. The mono carries the quarterly rhythm.
